strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and timely problem: how multiple auto-bidding campaigns (e.g., managed by a single large advertiser like Amazon/Temu or a third-party agency) can coordinate their bids in repeated auctions under Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints.

It provides a clean, exact theoretical characterization (Assumption 1) of the necessary and sufficient condition under which the simple highest-value-compete coordination mechanism reduces RoS violations for every individual bidder.

The theoretical results for mirror-descent auto-bidders are strong. The paper proves that coordination always improves total value (Theorem 4.1), and under Assumption 1, asymptotically achieves the optimal total value among all possible coordination mechanisms (Theorem 4.2).
The extension to non-i.i.d. valuations is comprehensive and makes the theoretical contributions more robust to real-world scenarios where bidders are heterogeneous.
The paper is very well-written, with clear proof sketches in the main body and detailed, rigorous proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The proposed coordination protocol requires the coalition members to fully share their private values to determine the highest-value bidder. In practice, if the coalition consists of independent advertisers managed by a third party, sharing exact private valuations may raise privacy or truthfulness concerns which are not fully addressed.

The assumption that outside bids are i.i.d. drawn from a static distribution is a simplification. In actual advertising markets, outside bidders are also likely to run dynamic auto-bidding algorithms, which could lead to complex feedback loops.

The evaluation on real-world data (iPinYou) is somewhat limited by the dataset's constraints. To evaluate their model, the authors had to build an empirical i.i.d. model by drawing from a common pool of winning prices, which reduces the dynamical realism of the real-world dataset experiment.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and novel problem: coordination among multiple auto-bidding campaigns (value maximizers with Return-on-Spend constraints) in repeated second-price auctions.

The theoretical contributions are robust, including a necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) under which coordination guarantees reduced RoS violations for every individual bidder, as well as showing that coordinated mirror-descent algorithms unconditionally improve the total value of the coalition.
The authors show the asymptotic optimality of the proposed simple 'highest-value-compete' coordination mechanism among all possible coordination mechanisms.
The extension to independent but non-identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) valuations makes the theoretical model much more realistic and widely applicable.
The paper is very well-written, with clean mathematical formulations and clear explanations of the proofs and intuition.
weaknesses: The proposed coordination mechanism requires complete information sharing of exact valuations among the coalition members at each round. In scenarios where different advertisers authorize a third-party agent, eliciting truthful private values might be strategic and incentive compatibility issues are not fully addressed.

The assumption that outside bids are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) ignores the potential feedback loop where outside bidders (who are also likely using auto-bidding algorithms) adjust their bids in response to the coalition's coordinated actions.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of the effects of coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints.
The identification of Assumption 1 as a necessary and sufficient condition for coordination to reduce RoS constraint violations is a nice theoretical contribution.
The authors provide extensions of their results to the non-i.i.d. case, establishing conditions under which coordination still yields benefits.
weaknesses: The proposed coordination mechanism (where only the highest-value bidder participates and others bid zero) is essentially a classic bidding ring or collusion cartel, which is well-studied in auction theory. Framing this classic cooperative mechanism as a novel contribution in the context of auto-bidding feels somewhat overstated.

The model assumes that bidders truthfully share their private valuations with a central coordinator. However, in many practical settings (such as multiple advertisers managed by a third-party agency), bidders may have strategic incentives to misreport their values to gain a larger share of the utility. The paper does not address the incentive compatibility of this information-sharing process.

The real-world data evaluation on the iPinYou dataset is severely limited. By aggregating winning prices into a common pool and sampling values i.i.d. with replacement, the authors discard the sequential, temporal, and bidder-specific characteristics of the real-world dataset, essentially treating it as synthetic data with an empirical marginal distribution.

In practice, ad campaigns almost always operate under budget constraints in addition to RoS constraints. Excluding budget constraints from the model significantly limits the practical applicability of the theoretical results.

The theoretical result (Theorem 4.2) showing that coordinated mirror-descent algorithms achieve the best possible value relies on the multipliers converging to 0, which implies that bidders submit arbitrarily high bids ($b \to \infty$). In actual advertising exchanges, bidding extremely high amounts is highly risky and can lead to catastrophic RoS violations if the market dynamics shift.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and relevant problem in modern online advertising: how to coordinate multiple bidding campaigns (managed by the same advertiser or a third-party agent) that act as value-maximizers under Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints.

The theoretical framework is rigorous. The paper successfully identifies a necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) under which coordination reduces RoS constraint violations for any weakly overbidding algorithm.

The paper provides strong convergence and optimality guarantees for a broad and popular class of online learning algorithms (mirror-descent based auto-bidders). Specifically, Theorem 4.1 shows coordination always improves total value, and Theorem 4.2 establishes its asymptotic optimality.
The authors extend their theoretical results to asymmetric (non-i.i.d.) settings, which is crucial for practical applications where campaigns have different valuation distributions.
The theoretical findings are backed by thorough empirical evaluation using both synthetic simulations and a widely used real-world dataset (iPinYou).
weaknesses: The entire theoretical analysis is framed around second-price auctions (SPA). While historically dominant, many modern advertising platforms (such as Google Ad Manager and AppNexus) have shifted to first-price auctions (FPA), limiting the direct applicability of the current results to those modern environments.

The model assumes that the coordinator has direct, truthful access to the private values of the participating bidders. In the collaborative bidding scenario with independent advertisers managed by a third-party agent, the bidders might have incentives to misreport their values, a challenge that is not formally addressed in the mechanism.
The paper focuses solely on RoS constraints and does not incorporate budget constraints, which are extremely common in practice and often interact dynamically with RoS constraints.

strengths: Novel and highly practical problem formulation: The paper shifts focus from the widely studied independent auto-bidding setting to coordinated auto-bidding. This is highly relevant to industry setups where agencies manage multiple campaigns or large advertisers run portfolios.

Rigorous and elegant theoretical results: The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violations. It also provides strong optimality results for mirror-descent algorithms.
Good generalization: The extension of the results from i.i.d. to non-i.i.d. settings (Section 5) adds robustness and practical value.

Thorough empirical validation: The authors complement their theoretical proofs with extensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets (iPinYou), demonstrating consistent and significant gains.
weaknesses: High information requirements for coordination: The studied coordination protocol requires knowing the exact values of all coalition members in each round to select the highest-value bidder. This central-coordinator assumption, while common, should be discussed in terms of communication overhead and privacy.

Asymptotic nature of the guarantees: Key optimality and convergence results (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 5.2) are asymptotic (as $T \to \infty$). Finite-time regret/utility bounds would significantly strengthen the results.

Static/i.i.d. outside bidders: The assumption that outside bids are drawn i.i.d. from a stationary distribution ignores the competitive response of other advertisers. If outside bidders are also adaptive, the dynamics of the system could change.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly relevant problem in modern digital advertising: coordinating value-maximizing auto-bidders under Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints.
Provides a solid and rigorous theoretical analysis, showing that coordination unconditionally increases the total value of coalition bidders running mirror descent.
Employs an elegant proof technique involving a virtual single-bidder relaxation and dual envelopes to bound independent bidding performance.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, clearly structured, and easy to follow, with detailed proofs provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The negative result in Theorem 3.1 relies on a highly pathological 'punishment' algorithm specifically constructed to fail under coordination. This makes the necessity of Assumption 1 less meaningful for practical learning algorithms, and it is unclear if realistic algorithms (like mirror descent) can ever be harmed by coordination when the assumption fails.

The paper assumes a central planner has access to the bidders' true private valuations, but completely ignores incentive compatibility. For coalitions of independent advertisers (Scenario 1), bidders would have strong incentives to misreport their values to be selected by the coordinator, which could collapse the mechanism.

The 'real-world' experiment on the iPinYou dataset is essentially an i.i.d. simulation using an empirical distribution of winning prices. It does not reflect true real-world bidding dynamics, temporal correlations, or strategic interactions.

The coordination mechanism itself is the classic, well-known cartel mechanism for second-price auctions (highest-value bidder bids, others bid 0). The novelty lies purely in the analysis under RoS constraints rather than any algorithmic or mechanism design innovation.
